requirements: The core contributions of TCL — an efficient and transferable DL compiler framework combining an RDU active-learning sampler, a Mamba-based cost model, and a continual knowledge distillation framework — have been reproduced.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware platforms, software environment, and TVM/Ansor integration required for TCL are available and configured.
Hardware platforms used across dataset-based and end-to-end experiments are available.

Code/documentation identifies the dataset-based training/eval server: Intel Xeon Silver 4214 CPU with 256 GB memory and four NVIDIA 32 GB V100 GPUs, and training scripts are runnable on such a machine (or a documented equivalent).
Code/documentation supports the end-to-end CPU platform (Intel i7-12700F) as the target CPU device for tuning and inference latency measurements.
Code/documentation supports the end-to-end GPU platform (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080Ti) as the target GPU device for tuning and inference latency measurements.

Configuration lists the six Tenset source hardware platforms used (Intel Platinum 8272CL, Intel E5-2673 v4, AMD EPYC 7452, ARM Graviton2, NVIDIA Tesla K80, NVIDIA Tesla T4) so that per-platform cost model training and CKD source selection are correctly routed.
The software stack for training cost models and for running end-to-end tuning is provisioned.
The cost-model training environment uses Python 3.8.0, PyTorch 1.7.0, CUDA 10.1.243, and cuDNN 7.6.0 (pinned via requirements/conda/Dockerfile).
The end-to-end tuning environment uses Python 3.8.20, PyTorch 1.8.0, CUDA 11.1, and cuDNN 8.2.0 (pinned via requirements/conda/Dockerfile).
The Mamba dependency (mamba-ssm and its selective_scan CUDA kernel, or equivalent SSM implementation) is installed and importable in the cost-model training environment.
GPU acceleration is verified in the training environment: a smoke test confirms that torch.cuda.is_available() is True and that a Mamba block forward pass runs on GPU without error.
TCL is integrated into TVM/Ansor so that the trained cost model drives the auto-tuning search on the target hardware.
TCL is integrated into TVM version 0.8.0, and the repository contains patches/scripts that build TVM 0.8.0 with the TCL cost model registered as a selectable auto-scheduler cost model.
The TCL cost model is registered as an Ansor XGBModel-compatible callback (predict / update interface) so that Ansor's search algorithm can query it during tuning.

Code has been implemented that uses Relay's operator fusion algorithm to partition input DNN models (PyTorch/TensorFlow/Keras/Caffe or ONNX) into Ansor-granularity computational subgraphs before tuning.

Code has been implemented for the end-to-end tuning loop that runs 2000 trials per model, invokes the TCL cost model for candidate scoring, dispatches measurements to the target hardware via Ansor's RPC/local runner, and records per-trial tuning time and best inference latency.

Code has been implemented that generates hardware code from the top-K selected schedule primitive sequences via TVM's codegen and executes the resulting tensor programs on the target CPU/GPU to obtain measured latency.
Reproducibility and training-schedule infrastructure is configured to match the paper's setup.

The training script exposes configurable optimizer/schedule parameters and defaults to Adam with initial learning rate 0.0007, batch size 1024, and 100 epochs with no early stopping for cost-model training.

The CKD training driver evenly divides the total epoch budget across hardware platforms and across CL/KD stages, applies cosine annealing with period 10 during CL and a stepwise decay of 0.1 every 5 epochs during KD, matching the paper's schedule.

Random seeds and measurement-averaging (multiple hardware measurements averaged per tensor program) are configurable and documented so that latency measurements are reproducible on the target hardware.
The Tenset dataset across six hardware platforms plus the newly collected Intel i7-12700F CPU and NVIDIA RTX 3080Ti GPU tensor program datasets are prepared, split, and ready for training/evaluation.

The Tenset open-source dataset covering six hardware platforms (Intel Platinum 8272CL, Intel Xeon E5-2673 v4, AMD EPYC 7452, ARM Graviton2, NVIDIA Tesla K80, NVIDIA Tesla T4) is downloaded and made available for training/evaluation.

Code has been implemented to download or reference the Tenset open-source dataset and organize per-hardware-platform tensor program data into a consistent on-disk directory structure indexed by platform name.

Code has been implemented that verifies the presence of all six Tenset hardware platforms (Intel Platinum 8272CL, Intel E5-2673 v4, AMD EPYC 7452, ARM Graviton2, NVIDIA Tesla K80, NVIDIA Tesla T4) and refuses to proceed if any platform's samples are missing.
Newly collected tensor program datasets on the Intel i7-12700F CPU and NVIDIA RTX 3080Ti GPU platforms are produced following the Tenset protocol.

Code has been implemented to collect tensor program measurement data on Intel i7-12700F CPU and NVIDIA RTX 3080Ti GPU using the same collection protocol as Tenset (same subgraph partitioning, schedule sampling, and measurement pipeline).
The measurement collection code averages multiple repeated measurements per tensor program to produce stable latency labels, matching the Tenset stability protocol.
The collected Intel i7-12700F CPU dataset contains approximately 8.65 million tensor program samples (matching the per-CPU-platform sample count reported in Section 7.1.1).
The collected NVIDIA RTX 3080Ti GPU dataset contains approximately 8.44 million tensor program samples (matching the per-GPU-platform sample count reported in Section 7.1.1).
The dataset covers the full set of neural network architectures and input configurations used in TCL evaluation.

The training/validation data includes tensor programs derived from the twelve architectures listed in Section 7.1.1: ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ResNeXt-50, Wide-ResNet50, MobileNetV2, MobileNetV3, InceptionV3, DenseNet-121, ResNet3D-18, VGG-16, BERT, and DCGAN.

Code has been implemented that uses Ansor's operator-fusion / Relay-based subgraph partitioning at the same granularity described in the paper, so tensor programs correspond to the intended assignment granularity.
Per-platform train/validation/test splits are constructed exactly as specified in Section 7.1.1.

Code has been implemented that designates a per-platform test set consisting of tensor programs from ResNet-50, MobileNet-V2, ResNeXt-50, BERT-tiny, and BERT-base at batch size 1, image size 224 for CNNs and sequence length 128 for BERT models.
Code has been implemented that splits the remaining (non-test) samples into training and validation sets with a 9:1 ratio for each platform, reproducibly (fixed seed).
The split logic ensures no leakage: the five test networks' subgraphs are entirely excluded from the train and validation sets on every platform.
Sampling-rate-based training subsets are producible from each platform's training data for RDU Sampler and ablation studies.
Code has been implemented that, given a target sampling rate (5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 50%, 70%, 90%), produces a labeled training subset drawn from a platform's training data.

A 10% subset of an Intel i7-12700F CPU platform's samples yields approximately 0.86 million tensor programs, and a 10% subset of the NVIDIA RTX 3080Ti GPU platform yields approximately 0.84 million tensor programs, matching the counts stated in Section 7.1.1.
Data loading pipelines produce inputs in the format expected by the Mamba-based cost model.

Code has been implemented for a data loader that yields batched (schedule-primitive-feature tensor, latency-label) pairs suitable for LambdaRank training, using the platform-appropriate feature dimensions (26×22 on CPU, 41×20 on GPU as described in Section 5.1).
The data loader groups tensor programs by subgraph/assignment so that LambdaRank-style ranking losses can be computed within groups and Top-k evaluation aggregates over subgraphs per model.
The TLP-based schedule-primitive feature extraction augmented with hardware-aware CPU/GPU features (26x22 for CPU, 41x20 for GPU) has been implemented as specified in Section 5.1 and Table 1.
Schedule-primitive extraction from tensor programs (TLP-style base features) has been implemented.

Code has been implemented to parse tensor programs and extract the ordered sequence of schedule primitives (e.g., SP/split, RE/reorder, FU/fuse, and other Ansor schedule primitives) that produced each program.

Code has been implemented to tokenize/encode each schedule primitive step into a fixed-length numerical feature vector following the TLP feature representation scheme (primitive type + operands/parameters).
The extracted base schedule-primitive features are hardware-independent (identical for the same tensor program regardless of target hardware) as required by the TLP baseline.
Hardware-aware feature augmentation for CPU and GPU platforms (per Table 1) has been implemented.

The CPU hardware feature vector includes the 11 fields specified in Table 1: Cores, Threads, Turbo frequency, Boost Frequency, L1 Cache, L2 Cache, L3 Cache, Max memory channels, Max memory capacity, Max memory bandwidth, and Bytes Size of SIMD Extensions.

The GPU hardware feature vector includes the 12 fields specified in Table 1: Cuda Cores, Base Clock, Boost Clock, Memory clock, Memory size, Memory bus width, Peak Memory bandwidth, FP64/FP32/FP16 Performance, and INT8/INT4 Performance.

A hardware-spec lookup / configuration file has been implemented that provides the correct numerical values of the Table 1 features for each supported platform (the four Tenset CPUs, Intel i7-12700F, the two Tenset GPUs, and NVIDIA RTX 3080Ti).

Code has been implemented to concatenate the hardware-aware features to each schedule-primitive step so that the combined per-step feature is used as input to the cost model (enabling cross-hardware transfer in the CKD framework).
The final per-tensor-program feature tensor has the exact shape stated in Section 5.1: 26x22 for CPU and 41x20 for GPU.
For CPU platforms, each schedule-primitive sequence produced by the feature extractor has shape (26, 22), i.e., 26 primitive steps with 22-dimensional per-step feature vectors.
For GPU platforms, each schedule-primitive sequence produced by the feature extractor has shape (41, 20), i.e., 41 primitive steps with 20-dimensional per-step feature vectors.
Sequences shorter than the required length (26 for CPU, 41 for GPU) are padded and sequences longer than the required length are truncated so that all outputs have the exact target shape.
The feature extractor produces consistent, reproducible outputs suitable for downstream cost-model training.

Code has been implemented to numerically normalize/encode feature values (e.g., primitive type IDs, operand magnitudes, hardware spec values) so the resulting tensors are directly consumable by the Mamba-based cost model without further preprocessing.

The feature extraction pipeline can be batch-applied to the full Tenset-scale dataset (~8.65M CPU / ~8.44M GPU samples per platform) and outputs are saved/loaded in a format compatible with the training pipeline.
Running the feature extractor twice on the same tensor program and hardware platform produces byte-identical feature tensors (deterministic extraction).
Ablation-style behavioral checks demonstrate that hardware-aware features (vs. hardware-independent TLP features) meaningfully change extractor outputs across platforms.

For the same tensor program encoded for two different CPU (or two different GPU) platforms, the extracted 26x22 (or 41x20) tensors differ only in the hardware-aware feature columns and are identical in the schedule-primitive columns.
The Mamba-based cost model architecture (encoder, Mamba block with SSM/selective mechanism, decoder) and the LambdaRank loss function have been implemented as described in Section 5.
The overall Mamba-based cost model architecture (encoder + normalization + Mamba block + normalization + decoder pipeline) matching Figure 5 has been implemented.

Code has been implemented that defines the encoder as three sequential linear layers with output dimensions 64, 128, and 128 mapping raw schedule-primitive features into a 128-dimensional hidden representation.
Code has been implemented that defines the decoder as three sequential linear layers with output dimensions 64, 32, and 1 producing a scalar prediction per tensor program.

Code has been implemented that applies RMSNorm (or an equivalent normalization) both before feeding the encoder output into the Mamba block and before feeding the Mamba block output into the decoder, as depicted in Figure 5.
Code has been implemented so that a full forward pass through the cost model preserves the sequence length of the input schedule-primitive tokens and outputs a scalar score per sequence.
The forward pass accepts CPU inputs of shape (batch, 26, 22) and GPU inputs of shape (batch, 41, 20) matching the feature dimensions described in Section 5.1.
The Mamba block with SSM and selective (input-dependent) mechanism has been implemented as the core sequence-modeling component of the cost model.

Code has been implemented for the Mamba block's input branch consisting of a linear projection followed by a depthwise 1D convolution and a SiLU activation before entering the SSM, matching the block diagram in Figure 5.
Code has been implemented for the Mamba block's gating branch consisting of a linear projection followed by a SiLU activation whose output is element-wise multiplied with the SSM output.

Code has been implemented that computes the discretized selective state-space update z_t = A_bar z_{t-1} + B_bar mu_t and y_t = C z_t (Eq. 4-5 discretized form), with A, B, C parameters and A serving as the NxN state transition matrix.
Code has been implemented so that the B, C, and step-size (Delta) parameters of the SSM are produced as input-dependent functions of the token features, realizing Mamba's selective mechanism.
Code has been implemented that exposes the Mamba hyperparameters n_layer, d_state, expand, and d_conv as configurable arguments of the Mamba block.
The default hyperparameter configuration of the Mamba block used for the main experiments is n_layer=1, d_state=8, expand=1, d_conv=4, matching the best combination reported in Table 2.
Code has been implemented so that the Mamba block's output has the same shape (batch, seq_len, hidden_dim) as its input, enabling the residual/normalization pipeline shown in Figure 5.
The LambdaRank loss function (Eq. 6-8 style) used to train the cost model to rank tensor programs by latency has been implemented.
Code has been implemented for the LambdaRank pairwise loss L = sum_{i,j} log(1 + exp(-sigma (s_i - s_j))) * |Delta NDCG(i,j)| over pairs within each ranking group (subgraph).
Code has been implemented that computes the gain function G_i = (2^{y_i} - 1) / maxDCG, where maxDCG is derived from the ideal ranking based on ground-truth latencies.
Code has been implemented that computes the discount factor D_i = log2(1 + i) and forms Delta NDCG(i,j) = |G_i - G_j| * |1/D_i - 1/D_j| as specified in Section 5.3.
The loss module groups candidate tensor programs by their subgraph/assignment such that ranking is computed within each group rather than across the whole batch.
The loss is selected/configured as LambdaRank (not MSE) in the training entry point for the Mamba-based cost model, matching the design choice in Section 5.3.
Training and inference behavior of the Mamba-based cost model is correctly wired for offline training on the tensor program dataset.
Code has been implemented that trains the cost model with the Adam optimizer at an initial learning rate of 0.0007, batch size 1024, for 100 epochs with no early stopping.
Code has been implemented that computes the Top-k score metric (Eq. 12) so that Top-1 and Top-5 scores can be reported on the held-out test set of five representative DNNs.
The trained Mamba-based cost model exposes an inference API returning a predicted score per candidate schedule-primitive sequence that can be plugged into Ansor/TVM's search loop.
Quantitative properties of the Mamba-based cost model reported in the paper are reproduced.
The serialized Mamba-based cost model (encoder + Mamba block + decoder) has a total on-disk size of approximately 0.35 MB, matching the size reported in Table 3.

When trained end-to-end on the full Tenset dataset for the Intel Xeon E5-2673 v4 CPU with the default hyperparameters, the Mamba-based cost model achieves a Top-1 score of approximately 0.9050 on the held-out five-model test set (matching Table 3).

When trained end-to-end on the full Tenset dataset for the NVIDIA T4 GPU with the default hyperparameters, the Mamba-based cost model achieves a Top-1 score of approximately 0.8891 on the held-out five-model test set (matching Table 3).

Training the cost model with the LambdaRank loss produces a strictly higher Top-1 score on at least one held-out platform than training the identical architecture with an MSE loss, supporting the design choice in Section 5.3.
The RDU active learning sampler that jointly optimizes representativeness, diversity, and uncertainty (Algorithm 1, Eqs. 1-3) has been implemented.
The Representativeness component enforcing operator-type distribution matching between sampled and full unlabeled data has been implemented.

Code has been implemented for a Calc_Dist function that iterates over all assignments in the unlabeled dataset D_u, extracts the operator type of each assignment via a get_op utility, tallies frequencies in freq_map, and returns a probs_map with per-operator probability = count / total_assignments (matching Algorithm 1 lines 1-12).

Code has been implemented that classifies each assignment into one of the operator-type categories shown in Figure 3 (e.g., conv, conv_relu, dwconv_relu, dense, matmul, avg_pool, gavg_pool, softmax, transconv_scale_relu, etc.) so that the representativeness distribution over the Tenset dataset can be computed.
Code has been implemented that, given a total sampling budget B_t, allocates a per-operator-type budget[op_type] = B_t * probability[op_type] using probs_map (Algorithm 1 lines 17-19).

Code has been implemented that enforces the per-operator budget during selection: when the top-scoring candidate's operator type has reached its budget (selected[T_op] >= budget[T_op]), the sample is skipped; otherwise it is added to D_l (Algorithm 1 lines 27-31).

After running the RDU sampler at 10% budget on the Tenset Intel Xeon E5-2673 CPU data, the operator-type distribution of the sampled assignments matches the reference distribution in Figure 3 within reasonable tolerance (relative frequency error <= 0.02 per operator type).
The Diversity component computing per-candidate distance scores over normalized cost-model predictions (Eq. 1) has been implemented.

Code has been implemented that normalizes cost-model predictions f(x_i) and f(x_j) prior to computing the distance score, matching the paper's statement that predictions are normalized before use in Eq. 1.

Code has been implemented that computes d_s(x_i) = min_{x_j in D_l} |f(x_i) - f(x_j)| for every unlabeled sample x_i (Eq. 1), i.e., the minimum absolute difference between the unlabeled candidate and each labeled program's normalized predicted score.

When two candidates have equal d_s values, code has been implemented that prefers the one with higher predicted performance f(x_i), consistent with the paper's tie-breaking rule and the weighting used in line 24 of Algorithm 1.
The Uncertainty component computing variance-based uncertainty scores (Eqs. 2-3) between each unlabeled candidate and the labeled pool has been implemented.
Code has been implemented that computes the mean predicted score mu(x_i) over pairwise comparisons between the unlabeled candidate x_i and each labeled sample x_j in D_l, following Eq. 2.
Code has been implemented that computes the variance-based uncertainty score u_s(x_i) using the deviations of the predictions from the mean mu(x_i) across labeled samples, following Eq. 3.

The uncertainty computation uses variance (regression-style) rather than classification-style entropy/confidence, consistent with the paper's statement that RDU treats sampling as a regression problem.
The overall RDU scoring, sample selection loop, and cost-model update procedure (Algorithm 1 lines 13-35) have been implemented.
Code has been implemented that initializes D_l with Rand_Select(D_u) and initializes the cost model f on this random seed set before the RDU iterative loop begins (Algorithm 1 lines 14-15).

Code has been implemented that computes the total per-candidate score t_s(x_i) = f(x_i) * d_s(x_i) + u_s(x_i) for every x_i in D_u (Algorithm 1 line 24), where f(x_i) weights the diversity term to prioritize high-performance candidates on ties.

Code has been implemented that in each inner iteration selects T_i = argmax_{x_i in D_u} t_s(x_i), moves it from D_u to D_l when its operator-type budget allows, and continues until the round budget S_t reaches B_t (Algorithm 1 lines 21-32).

Code has been implemented for an outer active-learning loop of T rounds where the cost model f is retrained/updated via f.update() at the end of each round on the accumulated labeled set D_l (Algorithm 1 lines 20, 33).

The RDU sampler exposes hyperparameters for total budget B_t (e.g., corresponding to 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 50%, 70%, 90% of the full dataset), number of rounds T, and the initial random seed-set size, so downstream sampling-rate studies can be run without code changes.
The behavior and outputs of the RDU sampler have been validated against expected properties.
Given a fixed random seed, the RDU sampler produces a deterministic, reproducible labeled set D_l for a given (D_u, B_t, T) triple.
The final |D_l| produced by the sampler equals the requested budget B_t within +/- 1 sample, and no operator type exceeds its allocated per-type budget.

On the Intel Xeon E5-2673 CPU dataset at 10% sampling, the normalized latency score distribution of the RDU-sampled set is more balanced than the full-dataset distribution shown in Figure 4 (specifically, the fraction of samples with normalized score > 0.5 is materially higher than the 8.1% observed in the full dataset), reflecting the diversity criterion.

At 10% sampling on the NVIDIA T4 GPU, a cost model trained on the RDU-selected data achieves Top-1 score approximately 0.8761 and Top-5 score approximately 0.9318 (matching Table 4 within tolerance), confirming the sampler's numerical claims against ALT/BALTO baselines.

At 10% sampling on the Intel Xeon E5-2673 CPU, a cost model trained on the RDU-selected data achieves Top-1 score approximately 0.8806 and Top-5 score approximately 0.9512 (matching Table 4 within tolerance).

The CKD framework with hardware knowledge base (KB) + hardware active column (AC), alternating CL and KD phases, progressive network connections, EWC forgetting prevention, and the loss functions (Eqs. 9-11) has been implemented.
The dual-branch KB + AC architecture, each instantiated from the Mamba-based cost model (encoder, Mamba block, decoder), has been implemented.
Code has been implemented that instantiates a hardware Knowledge Base (KB) as a Mamba-based cost model with the same encoder / Mamba block / decoder architecture as described in Fig. 5.
Code has been implemented that instantiates a hardware Active Column (AC) sharing the same Mamba-based encoder / Mamba block / decoder architecture as the KB.
The combined KB+AC model checkpoint size is approximately 0.7 MB as stated in Section 6.
Code has been implemented that exposes freeze/unfreeze operations on KB and AC parameter groups independently, so that only one branch is trainable at a time.
The progressive network connections that fuse per-layer KB activations into the corresponding AC layer via Eq. 9 have been implemented.
Code has been implemented that extracts per-layer activations h_i^{KB} from the KB's encoder layers, Mamba block, and decoder layers so they can be fed as lateral inputs to the AC.

The AC forward pass implements h_i^{AC} = sigma( W_i h_{i-1}^{AC} + b_i + U_i ( V_i (alpha_i ⊙ h_{i-1}^{KB}) + c_i ) ) with trainable alpha_i vector, weight matrices W_i, U_i, V_i and biases b_i, c_i as in Eq. 9.
The trainable gating vector alpha_i in the progressive connection has the same dimensionality as the number of units in layer i and is registered as a learnable parameter.
The nonlinear activation sigma applied after the progressive-connection linear combination is implemented consistently across AC layers.
The Continual Learning (CL) phase—KB frozen, AC trained on the new hardware with LambdaRank loss from Eq. 10—has been implemented.
During the CL phase, the KB parameters are frozen (requires_grad=False) and no gradients flow into KB weights.
The CL loss L_CL(p_t, l_t, theta) implements the LambdaRank loss on AC predictions p_t against target-hardware latency labels l_t as in Eq. 10.
During the CL stage the learning rate follows a cosine annealing schedule with period 10 as specified in Section 7.1.3.
The Knowledge Distillation (KD) phase—AC frozen as teacher, KB updated as student with the composite loss in Eq. 11 including EWC forgetting regularization—has been implemented.
During the KD phase, AC parameters are frozen and only KB parameters receive gradient updates.
The KD loss includes a student independent-learning term that measures the KB's prediction error against ground-truth labels P_G on each batch.

The KD loss includes a teacher distillation term that measures the discrepancy between student KB predictions P_S_j and teacher AC predictions P_T_j, weighted by the normalized teacher-loss score Phi_j per batch.
Phi_j is computed as the normalization of the teacher loss e_T across all batches of the dataset, so that batches with higher teacher error contribute proportionally less distillation weight.
The scalar beta that balances student loss and distillation loss is set to 0.5 as stated in Section 6.
During the KD stage the learning rate follows a stepwise decay of factor 0.1 every 5 epochs as specified in Section 7.1.3.
Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is used during the KD phase to prevent catastrophic forgetting of prior hardware knowledge in the KB.
Code has been implemented that computes and stores the Fisher information matrix F_{t,k} for each KB parameter k after learning the t-th hardware platform.
The EWC penalty term sum_k F_{t,k} (theta_k^{KB} - theta_{t,k}^{KB*})^2 is added to the KD loss as the third component of Eq. 11.
The EWC forgetting weight lambda is set to 10,000 as stated in Section 6.
After finishing the KD phase for hardware t, the current KB parameters are snapshotted as theta_{t}^{KB*} for use in the next platform's EWC penalty.
The alternating CL / KD training scheduler over an ordered sequence of source hardware platforms followed by the target platform has been implemented.

The training procedure iterates over source hardware platforms first and processes the target hardware platform last, matching the "source platform first, target platform last" order stated in Section 7.4.3.
For each source platform the framework runs a CL phase (AC training with KB frozen) immediately followed by a KD phase (KB training with AC frozen and EWC applied).
For the final target hardware platform only the CL phase is performed and no subsequent KD phase runs, as described in Section 7.4.3.
The total training epochs are evenly divided across the hardware platforms and across CL/KD stages as specified in Section 7.1.3.
Deterministic behavioral properties of the alternating CL/KD dynamics can be verified from the implementation.
During a CL phase, KB parameter tensors are byte-identical before and after the phase; during a KD phase, AC parameter tensors are byte-identical before and after the phase.
Before the target hardware's CL phase begins, the AC's Top-1 score on that target hardware is 0, reproducing the pre-CL flat segment of Fig. 8.
During a source-platform KD phase, the AC's Top-1 score on that source platform remains unchanged (AC frozen), reproducing the flat KD segments in Fig. 8.
The CKD framework integrates with the Mamba-based cost model and the RDU sampler at the target hardware to form the full TCL training pipeline.
Both KB and AC use the exact Mamba-based cost model architecture defined in Section 5.2 (encoder 64/128/128, Mamba block with chosen hyperparameters, decoder 64/32/1).
When training the cost model for the target hardware within CKD, the target-platform data is subsampled by the RDU Sampler (10% by default) before being fed into the AC's CL phase.
The CKD training loop uses the Adam optimizer with initial learning rate 0.0007 and batch size 1024 for 100 total epochs as specified in Section 7.1.3.

The Mamba hyperparameter sweep experiments (n_layer, d_state, expand, d_conv) reproducing Table 2 on Intel Xeon E5-2673 CPU and NVIDIA T4 GPU have been conducted and confirm the [1, 8, 1, 4] optimal setting.
The hyperparameter sweep infrastructure for the Mamba cost model is configured and runnable.

Code has been implemented that exposes n_layer, d_state, expand, and d_conv as configurable hyperparameters of the Mamba block used inside the cost model, so that each of the nine configurations in Table 2 can be instantiated by changing these arguments.

Code has been implemented that runs the Mamba cost model hyperparameter sweep for the nine (n_layer, d_state, expand, d_conv) configurations listed in Table 2 on both Intel Xeon E5-2673 CPU data and NVIDIA T4 GPU data.

The sweep uses the shared training protocol from Section 7.1.3 (Adam, learning rate 0.0007, batch size 1024, 100 epochs, LambdaRank loss, no early stopping) for every hyperparameter configuration on both E5-2673 and T4.

Code has been implemented that computes and logs Top-1 and Top-5 scores on the five-model test set (ResNet-50, MobileNet-V2, ResNeXt-50, BERT-tiny, BERT-base) for each hyperparameter configuration and each of the two platforms, matching the reporting format of Table 2.

Configurations that fail to converge (as reported by 'N/A' entries in Table 2 for Intel E5-2673 with (2,8,1,4) and (3,8,1,4)) are detected and marked as non-converged rather than reported as valid Top-k scores.
Layer-count (n_layer) sweep at d_state=8, expand=1, d_conv=4 reproduces Table 2 rows for n_layer in {1, 2, 3}.
The measured Top-1 score of the Mamba cost model with (n_layer, d_state, expand, d_conv) = (2, 8, 1, 4) on NVIDIA T4 matches the value 0.8512 reported in Table 2 within tolerance.
The measured Top-5 score of the Mamba cost model with (n_layer, d_state, expand, d_conv) = (2, 8, 1, 4) on NVIDIA T4 matches the value 0.9314 reported in Table 2 within tolerance.
The measured Top-1 score of the Mamba cost model with (n_layer, d_state, expand, d_conv) = (3, 8, 1, 4) on NVIDIA T4 matches the value 0.8458 reported in Table 2 within tolerance.
The Mamba cost model configurations (2, 8, 1, 4) and (3, 8, 1, 4) are observed to fail to converge on the Intel Xeon E5-2673 CPU dataset, matching the 'N/A' entries in Table 2.
State-expansion (d_state) sweep at n_layer=1, expand=1, d_conv=4 reproduces Table 2 rows for d_state in {8, 16, 32}.
The measured Top-1 score of the Mamba cost model with (1, 32, 1, 4) on NVIDIA T4 matches the value 0.856 reported in Table 2 within tolerance.
The measured Top-1 score of the Mamba cost model with (1, 16, 1, 4) on NVIDIA T4 matches the value 0.8848 reported in Table 2 within tolerance.
The measured Top-1 scores of the Mamba cost model with (1, 32, 1, 4) and (1, 16, 1, 4) on Intel Xeon E5-2673 match the values 0.8913 and 0.8530 respectively as reported in Table 2 within tolerance.
Block-expansion (expand) sweep at n_layer=1, d_state=8, d_conv=4 reproduces Table 2 rows for expand in {1, 2, 3}.
The measured Top-1 score of the Mamba cost model with (1, 8, 2, 4) on NVIDIA T4 matches the value 0.874 reported in Table 2 within tolerance.
The measured Top-1 score of the Mamba cost model with (1, 8, 3, 4) on NVIDIA T4 matches the value 0.8654 reported in Table 2 within tolerance.
The measured Top-1 scores of the Mamba cost model with (1, 8, 2, 4) and (1, 8, 3, 4) on Intel Xeon E5-2673 match the values 0.8903 and 0.8839 respectively as reported in Table 2 within tolerance.
Convolution-width (d_conv) sweep at n_layer=1, d_state=8, expand=1 reproduces Table 2 rows for d_conv in {2, 3, 4}.
